https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/23/mike.text: Menü Kereső Kijevben találkozott Mike Pence és Zelenszkij, Ukrajna szerint az USA Patriot-készletének 5 százalékával átvészelhetnék a telet Külföld Bánáti Anna Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kijevben találkozott Mike Pence korábbi amerikai alelnök és Volodimir Zelenszkij vasárnap, Pence a találkozó után arról nyilatkozott, hogy az ukrán elnök az USA-tól a fennmaradó Patriot-készletének mintegy 5 százalékát kérte, írja a Politico . Pence az ukrán függetlenség napja (augusztus 24.) alkalmából rendezett imareggelin vett részt Ukrajnában. Pence Kijevből azt nyilatkozta a CNN „State of the Union” című műsorában , hogy Ukrajna „nyerőfélben van” Oroszországgal szemben, de Zelenszkij aggodalmát fejezte ki a közelgő tél miatt. A volt alelnök azt mondta, Zelenszkij „egy dolgot világosan kifejtett” neki. „Mégpedig azt, hogy teljes mértékben arra számít, hogy a tél közeledtével – és ez inkább hamarabb, mint később fog bekövetkezni – Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök nem csupán iskolákat és gyerekkórházakat fog támadni, ahogy azt a héten tette, és nem csupán bevásárlóközpontot, ahol több mint tucatnyi ember vesztette életét, hanem az energiainfrastruktúrát is támadni fogja, hogy a zord téli hideget rákényszerítse az ukrán népre.” Pence szerint Zelenszkij azt mondta neki, hogy ha az USA átadná rakétavédelmi rendszerének 5 százalékát, az elég lehetne a téli hónapok átvészelésére. Az Iránnal folytatott háború azonban alaposan leszívta az Egyesült Államok készleteit, a gyártás felfuttatása pedig akár évekig is eltarthat, jelenleg különböző országok sora várja, hogy hozzájusson a megrendeléséhez . Augusztus 23-án észak-európai és balti országok vezetői is Kijevbe érkeztek , hogy támogatásukról biztosítsák Ukrajnát, illetve tárgyaljanak Zelenszkijjel a tettre készek koalíciójával való augusztus 24-i találkozó előtt. Zelenszkij Finnországgal megállapodott egy védelmiipari együttműködésről. Ukrajnának nyár elejére kritikusan kevés Patriot elfogórakétája maradt , pedig ezek jelentenék az egyetlen igazán hatékony védelmet az orosz ballisztikus rakétákkal szemben. A hiányt Oroszország egyre kegyetlenebbül kihasználja, Moszkva ma leginkább ballisztikus rakétákra építi az ukrán városok elleni éjszakai támadásait, a gyors, nehezen elfogható Iszkandereket és az Észak-Koreától beszerzett KN–23-asokat drónokkal és más rakétákkal együtt veti be. Nemrég helyszíni riportban mutattuk be, hogyan próbálják átaludni a támadásokkal tűzdelt, egyre több civil áldozatot követelő orosz támadásokat a Kijevben élők . https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/14/hout.text: Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthis captured more islands in the southern Red Sea, government and Houthi officials said Monday, strengthening their control of a major maritime shipping route.The capture of the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish is the latest in the group's swift advance around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key passage for oil shipments that has become even more crucial during the Iran war as the Strait of Hormuz remains under US and Iranian blockades.Like Hormuz, located at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula — is a chokepoint that connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea, making it a key waterway for cargo traffic to the Mediterranean Sea.For more than a month, the Houthis have been striking Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, stepping up pressure on global oil prices and boosting Iran's leverage in its war with the US.Forces of the internationally recognised Yemeni government have been attempting to rally and fight back, but the Houthi gains have seemingly come with little resistance.The Houthis deployed on the Hanish islands, 160 kilometres north of Bab el-Mandeb, after hundreds of government-allied forces withdrew from the archipelago, according to two government officials and a Houthi official.The group officially known as Ansar Allah captured the archipelago after seizing the nearby mainland port city of Mokha and the island of Perim, inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.In parallel, they waged an offensive further inland, particularly in the longtime battleground province of Taiz.The Houthis also launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets on Monday.The Houthis said they fired dozens of drones and missiles at the kingdom — which backs the Yemeni government — prompting the Saudi Civil Defence to issue brief alerts in the neighbouring cities of Khamis Mushait and Abha.The Saudi Civil Defence overnight said a Houthi projectile fell in a different area near the border with Yemen along the Red Sea, injuring two people and damaging a mosque and several other buildings.Riyadh did not announce any new attacks targeting the Houthis.Thousands fleeing fighting in YemenThe Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July after a UN truce that had largely maintained quiet since 2022, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport, prompting the Houthis to declare a blockade on the kingdom targeting its oil trade in July.Some 150 civilians have been killed in fighting since 3 September, the government's Human Rights Ministry said. More than 200 civilians have been wounded, it said.Thousands of families have fled their homes in Taiz and nearby provinces in the past day alone, said Khanzad Shah, acting head of Islamic Relief, a charity that operates in the area."Many of them don't have enough food or water as they had to flee with whatever they could carry. In some areas, whole villages have reportedly emptied," he said.The UN has estimated that more than 80,000 people have been displaced in the past two weeks, including over 2,000 people who fled by boat to Djibouti.The fighting threatens to reignite a war that for more than a decade brought disaster to Yemen, killing more than 150,000 people and driving the country to the brink of famine.The internationally recognised government supported by an array of disparate militias controls the south and east, including the key southern port of Aden.The Hanish islands, newly captured by the Houthis, had been controlled by the UAE-backed allies. However, the UAE dismantled its military infrastructure there earlier this year.For years, Saudi Arabia waged an air campaign against the Houthis, while backing the government and allied militias, yet it has appeared reluctant to throw itself fully back into the war, despite the Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and shipping.The Houthis are tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.Yemeni government forces to regroup?On Sunday, the Yemeni government's military said it launched airstrikes on Houthi positions in the port city of Mokha, the coastal town of Dhubab and elsewhere in Taiz province.The Houthis reported strikes by the Saudi-backed forces in Taiz province and artillery shelling in Saada province, the birthplace of the Houthi movement on Yemen's northern border with Saudi Arabia.Sultan al-Arada, a member of the government's presidential leadership council, described the collapse of government forces in Mokha, about 80 kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and elsewhere on Yemen's west coast as "painful and regrettable."He said in a televised interview aired late Saturday that forces "are currently regrouping and will return to the battle."Rashad al-Alimi, who leads the presidential council, sought on Sunday to downplay the defeats as "incidental," according to comments published by the country's state-run SABA news agency.The government "will remain clear and fixed on the goal of retrieving institutions and of reclaiming sovereignty over all national territories," al-Alimi said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cwvgde.text: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Close US President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire". Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me". Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections. The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election. More on this story. https://www.politico.eu/article/ecb-pres.text: Christine Lagarde said she will step down as president of the European Central Bank on Feb. 7, creating a vacancy at the top of one of Europe’s most powerful institutions and fueling further speculation about a possible return to French politics. An official familiar with Lagarde’s thinking, granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter, said she made her move now, almost a full year before the end of her term, to have “greater freedom to express her views and to engage in non-monetary matters, because she cannot remain neutral when she sees the developments taking place in her own country and in the world.” The ECB said in a statement only that Lagarde had informed European Council President António Costa of the decision earlier on Thursday. Advertisement Advertisement The announcement clears the way for a package deal among EU capitals over at least three appointments to the ECB’s six-strong Executive Board. Isabel Schnabel, head of the Bank’s markets department, is due to leave in January to take a senior role at the International Monetary Fund, while Philip Lane is due to depart the influential chief economist’s position in May. Negotiations over the appointments are likely to be intense, given the ECB’s vital influence in international markets, and the never-ending pressure on European government finances . Former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos, who heads the Bank for International Settlements, are seen as the two frontrunners in the race for the top job. The timing of the announcement means that President Emmanuel Macron will have a say in choosing Lagarde’s successor before he himself leaves office next spring . Marine Le Pen, the National Rally leader and a longtime critic of the EU, is currently well ahead in the polls to win the French presidency, and may take a radically different view about who should lead the ECB. “The EU is trying to guard at least somewhat against the risk that right-wing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election,” said Berenberg Bank’s head of research Holger Schmieding. Speculation has long swirled that Lagarde, formerly finance minister under President Nicolas Sarkozy, may throw herself back into French politics. She has stressed the need for “a pro-European voice” in the French elections, while still being consistently coy about running herself. Thursday’s announcement comes at a time when candidates from mainstream camps in France are all losing ground to far-left hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who wants the ECB to "set fire" to its French debt holdings . None looks likely to make the final round of the presidential election in May. Whoever follows her as ECB president will inherit an increasingly tense situation in Europe’s bond markets, where borrowing costs are hitting their highest level in years due to a cocktail of war-fueled inflation, demographics and competition from capital from Big Tech companies chasing AI-related riches. Advertisement Advertisement The problems are particularly acute in France, the eurozone’s second-largest economy, which faces a political impasse and mounting pressure over its public debt. Lagarde succeeded Mario Draghi at the ECB in 2019, after leading the International Monetary Fund and, in her time in office, has been a stalwart of the centrist mainstream that is now being squeezed by both wings of the political spectrum across Europe. “Christine Lagarde has led the European Central Bank through difficult times,” German finance minister Lars Klingbeil said in a statement. “Under her leadership, the ECB has kept the euro stable even during crises: when the coronavirus pandemic hit Europe hard, when Russia invaded Ukraine, and most recently in the face of the economic shocks caused by the war in Iran.” “Christine Lagarde's tenure at the helm of the ECB has only strengthened the confidence in the European single currency,” Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis said in a statement, promising to give the council a “swift” recommendation on the succession to heads of government. The ECB gave no details about Lagarde’s plans after leaving Frankfurt. However, she has talked to the World Economic Forum about taking over as chair, according to its founder Klaus Schwab. Reuters reported that the organizer of Davos could announce her appointment as early as this month. This story has been updated.
